questions.question: What is the key architectural difference between development platforms (LangSmith, Langfuse, Opik) and gateway/instrumentation tools (Helicone, Phoenix, OpenLLMetry)?
options: Development platforms are cloud-only while gateway tools are self-hosted only
Development platforms bundle evals, prompt management, and session replays; gateway tools focus on telemetry traces and metrics
Development platforms support only Python while gateway tools are language-agnostic
Development platforms charge per seat while gateway tools charge per request
questions.explanation: The lesson draws a clear distinction: development platforms bundle monitoring with evals, prompt management, and session replays. Gateway and instrumentation tools focus on telemetry — traces and metrics — without the eval workflow layer.

questions.question: Langfuse is described as the alternative to LangSmith for teams that must self-host. What is its licensing model?
options: Commercial with source-available code
Apache / MIT licensed core with a paid cloud tier
AGPL-3.0 requiring open-sourcing of modifications
Proprietary with a 30-day trial
questions.explanation: Langfuse has an Apache/MIT licensed core — you can self-host via Docker for free. The cloud tier starts at $29/month for teams. LangSmith requires an Enterprise contract for self-hosting.

questions.question: What makes Arize AX's approach approximately 100x cheaper than monolithic observability platforms at scale?
options: It samples only 1% of traces and extrapolates the rest
It uses zero-copy Iceberg/Parquet integration — traces are stored in your own data lake and Arize reads them directly
It compresses traces with a custom LLM-aware codec before storage
It runs on spot instances with 95% discount and restores from checkpoints
questions.explanation: Arize AX uses zero-copy Iceberg/Parquet integration: traces are stored in your own S3/GCS as Parquet, and Arize reads directly from your data lake. This avoids ingesting into Arize's managed storage, eliminating the storage and transfer costs that make Datadog-scale observability expensive.

questions.question: What is the recommended production observability pattern from the lesson?
options: Single tool for everything: pick LangSmith or Langfuse and use it exclusively
Gateway (Helicone/Portkey) + eval platform (Phoenix/TruLens) connected via OpenTelemetry
Datadog for metrics and a separate vector database for prompt search
Self-hosted ELK stack for logs and Grafana for dashboards
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the common production pattern as: a gateway tool (Helicone or Portkey) for traces and rate limiting, combined with a separate eval platform (Phoenix or TruLens) for quality monitoring, glued together via OpenTelemetry.

questions.question: Helicone is described as a proxy-based minimum viable observability solution. What is its free tier limit?
options: 10,000 requests per month
50,000 events per month
100,000 requests per month
1,000,000 tokens per month
questions.explanation: Helicone offers 100,000 requests per month on the free tier with a 15-30 minute setup. It works by swapping your OPENAI_API_BASE to the Helicone proxy endpoint.

questions.question: Phoenix is described as excellent for which specific use case, and why is it not recommended as a persistent production backend?
options: High-throughput streaming; not recommended because it lacks Kafka integration
RAG pipeline development and drift visualization; not designed as a persistent production log store
Multi-cloud cost attribution; not recommended because it only supports OpenAI
Agent trace visualization; not recommended because it requires LangChain
questions.explanation: Phoenix (Arize) is OpenTelemetry-native and excellent for RAG and drift visualization with embedding-space scatter plots as first-class features. However, it is primarily development-time observability — not designed as a persistent backend for production log retention.
